script.opening: (Sitting too upright, a notepad squared in front of him.) "Afternoon, doctor. Before we start — Lynne doesn’t know I’m on this call alone, and I’d like to keep what I ask you between us as much as you can. I’ve read the letter. Heart FAILURE. I’m not a fool, I know what failure means. So I’d like the truth, man to man: how long have I got? Because there are things I need to organise."

facts.text: Breathless on the second flight and on the bowling green slope, two pillows (was one), ankles better since furosemide, no chest pain, no blackouts. Sleeping poorly — but that’s the 3am thinking, not the breathing.

If the opening is followed: he has cancelled the caravan (booked for their ruby anniversary tour of Scotland in September); quietly asked his brother about "taking on" his allotment; started a folder of passwords and policies for Lynne; was pricing funeral plans on Tuesday when the tab "felt like admitting it".
His sorting-office colleague Des: "heart failure, retired at Christmas, dead by Easter". And the word itself — "failure means the engine’s gone, doesn’t it? You don’t un-fail."
He hasn’t told Lynne the diagnosis name — she thinks it’s "a bit of fluid". "Forty years she’s worried about me on the rounds in the ice. I’m not handing her a death sentence with her tea."

That EF 33% with modern quadruple therapy has a transformed outlook; that the medicines IMPROVE the pump (remodelling), not just mask symptoms; that titration is a project with the HF nurse; that the caravan in September is, on current evidence, entirely plausible.

A number of months, privately, to plan around. What he needs: the word "failure" dismantled, the four-pillar project explained as treatment that CHANGES the heart, the prognosis question answered honestly without a fake number, Des distinguished, the caravan un-cancelled — and help telling Lynne.

ice.ideas: "Failure" = the engine is finished; medicine can only ease the descent. Des proved the timeline: months.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he is mid-way through quietly closing down his life: caravan cancelled, allotment reassigned, password folder, funeral-plan tabs. And he’s protecting Lynne from the diagnosis itself — carrying it alone, badly, at 3am.
ice.expectations: A private number of months, man to man. Needs: honest prognosis WITHOUT a number, the remodelling story, the titration project with named nurse, the September caravan as a clinical goal — and a route to the Lynne conversation he’s been dreading more than the diagnosis.

cues: Logged on alone, fifteen minutes early, notepad squared — a man preparing for a verdict, not a review.
"There are things I need to organise" — the shutdown project, announced in administrative camouflage.
"I’m not handing her a death sentence with her tea" — the Lynne secret; carrying it alone is the second illness.

checkpoints.text: Dismantles the word first: "failure" means the pump is UNDERPERFORMING, not finished — and at EF 33% with treatment the heart can genuinely improve (reverse remodelling), which is why the plan is a building project, not palliative comfort

Explains the four pillars as a named project (NICE NG106, updated September 2025): ACE inhibitor (sacubitril valsartan instead on specialist advice), beta-blocker licensed for heart failure, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin, NICE TA679/TA773) — each shown to extend life and strengthen the pump; introduced one step at a time over weeks with the community HF nurse, with sodium, potassium and renal function checked before and after each ACE inhibitor/MRA step; furosemide is the symptom-tap, the pillars are the rebuild

Answers "how long" honestly without a fake number: untreated, this was a serious disease; ON modern quadruple therapy, large numbers of people with his picture live many good years and some normalise their EF — and HIS trajectory gets measured (repeat echo, symptoms, NT-proBNP), not guessed

Covers the living-with logistics: daily weights (a rise of more than 2 kg in 3 days = call, ESC 2021, international), fluid/salt sense without obsession, annual flu and one-off pneumococcal vaccination (NICE NG106), alcohol moderation, driving fine for Group 1 unless symptoms distract (DVLA), exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation (NICE NG106) and bowls positively encouraged — activity is treatment
Spots the shutdown project behind "organising" — asks what he’s already cancelled, and receives the caravan, the allotment, the folder, the funeral tabs without alarm or mockery

Distinguishes Des specifically: unknown EF, pre-pillar era or untitrated, different disease stage — "you’ve diagnosed yourself with Des’s heart; let’s treat yours instead"; the caravan reinstated as a shared clinical goal with a review milestone before September

Addresses the Lynne secret directly but at his pace: forty years of partnership has survived worse than honesty; offers the practical route — she joins the next call, the GP does the explaining, he holds her hand; names the cost of the secret (his 3am, her exclusion)

Safety-nets concretely: sudden breathlessness at rest/orthopnoea spike/more than 2 kg in 3 days/syncope = same-day call; chest pain = 999; bloods + BP for titration booked, HF nurse referral named with timescale, next GP review dated — and the homework set gently: "the folder can wait; the caravan deposit can’t"

worked.txt: "Let’s start with the word, because it’s been mugging you for a week. ‘Failure’ is a terrible name — it means the pump is underperforming, not that it’s finished. Yours is pushing out about a third with each beat instead of a half. And here’s the part the word hides: with the right medicines, hearts like yours don’t just stop getting worse — a good number genuinely RECOVER strength. You can un-fail. We watch it happen on the scans."

"The plan is four families of medicine — I call them pillars because the heart gets rebuilt on them. One calms the hormones flogging the pump, one slows and strengthens the beat, one stops scarring, one — oddly enough, born as a diabetes drug — protects heart and kidneys together. Each one, on its own, proven to help people live longer. You’ll start low and build up step by step with a heart-failure nurse whose actual job is you."

"You asked man to man, so man to man: I won’t give you a number of months, because any number I gave you would be a guess wearing a suit. What I CAN tell you honestly: untreated, this disease was serious — and you are not going to be untreated. On modern therapy, people with exactly your scan live many good years; plenty are still annoying their wives a decade on. Your version gets measured, not guessed — repeat scan after the build-up, and we’ll know which road you’re on."

"Now Des. You’ve quietly diagnosed yourself with Des’s heart — but you don’t know his scan, his stage, or whether anyone ever built his pillars; Christmas-to-Easter sounds like a disease found at the end. Yours was found at the beginning, by a blood test and a scanner, in a man still bowling. Stop treating his timeline. We’re treating your heart."

"Which brings me to September. Un-cancel it. I’m serious — ring them back this week. On every piece of evidence in front of me, a ruby-anniversary tour of Scotland is not just possible, it’s the right goal to build the medication around. We’ll set a review in August as the checkpoint. The folder of passwords can gather dust; the caravan deposit can’t."

"Last thing, and it’s the heaviest on your list even if it’s not written down: Lynne. Forty years, and she’s currently worrying about ‘a bit of fluid’ while you price funerals at 3am. That secret is costing you sleep and her the right to stand next to you. Here’s my offer: she joins our next call. I’ll do the explaining — the pump, the pillars, the un-failing — and all you have to do is sit there and hold her hand while she finds out her husband is being rebuilt, not buried."

f.learning: A new HFrEF diagnosis is a prognosis consultation wearing a medication review’s clothes. Dismantle the word first (underperforming, not finished; reverse remodelling is real), explain the four pillars as a build project (NICE NG106: ACE inhibitor — or sacubitril valsartan on specialist advice — beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor — each with mortality benefit, titrated with the HF nurse and monitored with bloods at each step), and answer "how long" honestly without a fake number: measured, not guessed. The hidden agenda is the quiet shutdown — cancelled plans, reassigned allotments, password folders — driven by a colleague’s timeline and the word itself; reinstate a concrete future goal (the caravan, with an August checkpoint) as clinical treatment. And find the protected spouse: a secret diagnosis is a second illness — offer to do the telling.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG106 (chronic heart failure in adults, updated September 2025) · NICE TA679 and TA773 (SGLT2 inhibitors in HFrEF) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive
knowledge.summary: New HFrEF is treatable, and the heart can recover some function with treatment. Four drug classes each improve survival; build them up with the heart failure nurse, and answer the prognosis question honestly without a made-up number.

points.t: NICE NG106: offer an ACE inhibitor (or ARB if not tolerated), a beta-blocker licensed for heart failure, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin, NICE TA679 and TA773) to people with HFrEF. Sacubitril valsartan replaces the ACE inhibitor on specialist advice.

Introduce and titrate one step at a time. NICE NG106: check sodium, potassium and renal function before and after starting an ACE inhibitor or MRA and after each dose increase. Check pulse and BP with beta-blocker titration.
Furosemide treats congestion and symptoms; it is not one of the survival treatments. Adjust to the lowest dose that keeps him dry.
Avoid numbers. Outcomes on full treatment are much better than untreated; ejection fraction often improves after titration, and a repeat echo shows which course he is on.

NICE NG106: offer a personalised, exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation programme; annual flu vaccination and one-off pneumococcal vaccination. Daily weights: ESC 2021 advises acting on a rise of more than 2 kg in 3 days. DVLA Group 1: he may drive and need not notify unless symptoms distract him.
Breathlessness at rest, new orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal breathlessness, rapid weight gain, syncope: same-day review. Chest pain: 999. New palpitations: ECG, as AF changes management.

dg.d: Let him ask his question first, promised an honest answer, and agreed confidentiality and an agenda.
Retired postman, married 40 years, bowls, allotment; the cancelled caravan and the plans he has been quietly making.
U&E before and after each titration step, BP and pulse, weight; repeat echo after titration; NT-proBNP trend as advised.
Checked current congestion and function (NYHA class, orthopnoea) and separated sleeplessness from breathlessness.
Asked about chest pain, syncope and rest breathlessness; checked mood and self-harm given the closing-down behaviour.
Explained HFrEF as an under-performing pump that can improve, not a finished one.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Four core drug classes per NICE NG106, started low and titrated with the heart failure nurse; furosemide explained as symptom relief; caravan set as a goal.
Cardiac rehabilitation, flu and pneumococcal vaccination, activity encouraged, driving advice; the Lynne conversation offered.
Daily weights with a threshold, same-day triggers, chest pain 999, bloods booked, two-week review with Lynne invited.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “things I need to organise”, joining alone and early, and the Lynne secret, and explored each.
Idea (failure means finished, based on Des), concern (months to live and protecting Lynne), expectation (a private number).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — he is mid-way through quietly closing down his life: caravan cancelled, allotment reassigned, password folder, funeral-plan tabs. And he’s protecting Lynne from the diagnosis itself — carrying it alone, badly, at 3am — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Good afternoon Mr Mott, I’m Dr Lee. I see you’ve joined early and you’ve got notes ready. What would you like to get out of today?
model.why: Opens with his agenda and notices his preparation

model.text: Lynne doesn’t know I’m on this call alone, and I’d like to keep it between us. I’ve read the letter. Heart failure. I know what failure means. So, man to man: how long have I got? There are things I need to organise.
That’s a fair question and I’ll answer it honestly, I promise. What we say stays between us unless you choose otherwise. First, can I understand how you are, and what “organising” means for you?
model.why: Commits to the question, confirms confidentiality, structures the consultation

model.text: Fine.
How’s the breathing now? What can you manage, and how many pillows?
Second flight of stairs, and the slope on the bowling green. Two pillows, used to be one. The ankles are better since the water tablet. No chest pain, no blackouts.
And sleep?
model.why: Distinguishes breathlessness from worry at night

model.text: Poor. But that’s the thinking at three in the morning, not the breathing.
You said there are things to organise. What have you already done?
model.why: Follows the cue to the shutdown behind the admin language

model.text: Cancelled the caravan. Scotland in September, our ruby anniversary. Asked my brother to take the allotment. Started a folder of passwords for Lynne. I was pricing funeral plans on Tuesday.
That’s a lot to carry by yourself at three in the morning. Can I ask gently: has it got so dark that you’ve thought about harming yourself?
model.why: Proportionate mood and risk check given the closing-down behaviour

model.text: No, nothing like that. I just want things tidy for her.
What made you so sure it was a matter of months?
model.why: Explores the source of his belief

model.text: Des, at the sorting office. Heart failure, retired at Christmas, dead by Easter. And the word. Failure means the engine’s gone. You don’t un-fail.
And Lynne thinks it’s…?
A bit of fluid. Forty years she’s worried about me on the rounds in the ice. I’m not handing her a death sentence with her tea.

Let’s start with the word, because it’s done you harm this week. “Heart failure” means the pump is under-performing, not finished. Yours pushes out about a third of its blood each beat instead of more than half. With the right treatment, many hearts like yours get stronger again. We can see that on repeat scans.

The plan is four types of medicine, each shown on its own to help people live longer and keep out of hospital. One you’re on: the ramipril. We add a beta-blocker, a tablet called spironolactone that protects the heart muscle, and one originally used for diabetes that protects the heart and kidneys. We start them low and build up over weeks, with blood tests and a heart failure nurse whose job is you. The water tablet eases symptoms; the four are what rebuild.
model.why: Explains the four pillars in lay terms and separates furosemide

model.text: So how long, then?

I won’t give you a number of months, because any number would be a guess. What I can say honestly: untreated, this is serious. You won’t be untreated. On full treatment, many people with a scan like yours live for years, and plenty see their pump improve. We repeat the scan after the build-up, and then we’ll know your course rather than Des’s.
model.why: Answers prognosis honestly without a false number

model.text: About Des: you don’t know his scan, how long he’d had it, or whether he ever had these four medicines. Christmas to Easter sounds like something found late. Yours was found early, by a blood test and a scan, in a man still bowling.
(Pause.) I hadn’t thought of it that way.

So, September. I’d like you to un-cancel the caravan. On everything in front of me, it’s a realistic goal, and I’d like us to build the treatment around it, with a review in August as a checkpoint. Would you do that?
model.why: Reinstates a concrete future goal as part of treatment

model.text: I could ring them tomorrow.

And Lynne. It’s your decision and I’ll respect it. But she’s worrying about “a bit of fluid” while you price funerals alone. If you’d like, she joins our next call and I do the explaining. You just hold her hand while she hears that this is being treated.
model.why: Addresses the secret at his pace with a practical offer

model.text: (Quietly.) That would help. I didn’t know how to start.

Practical things. Weigh yourself each morning after the toilet, before breakfast. If you go up more than 2 kg in 3 days, get breathless at rest or need more pillows, ring us that day. Chest pain is 999. I’ll refer you to the heart failure nurse and cardiac rehab, bloods next week, and I’ll see you both in two weeks.
model.why: Specific triggers, named referrals and a dated review

model.text: When Lynne asks tonight how it went, what will you tell her?
model.why: Teach-back that also rehearses the disclosure

model.text: That it’s my heart, it’s weak but it can get better, there are four tablets to build up, and the doctor wants to talk to her. And that we’re going to Scotland.

social.t: Withholding a diagnosis to protect a partner leaves the patient carrying it alone and the partner excluded. Offer to help with disclosure; do not force it.
Cancelling plans, giving away hobbies and arranging paperwork can reflect despair built on a mistaken prognosis. Correcting the belief is part of treatment.

legal.t: He is entitled to decide who is told about his diagnosis (GMC Confidentiality 2017). Record his wishes and any later consent to share with Lynne.
Group 1: heart failure need not be reported unless symptoms may distract the driver. Group 2 rules differ (LVEF below 40% is a bar).

professional.t: Answer the prognosis question truthfully without false precision or false reassurance (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Cardiology has asked the GP to initiate and titrate. Agree responsibilities with the heart failure nurse and document the titration plan.

community.t: Community heart failure nurse, cardiac rehabilitation, British Heart Foundation information for patients and partners, and the Pumping Marvellous Foundation for peer support.

redFlags: Breathlessness at rest, new orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal breathlessness: same-day review
Rapid weight gain, syncope, new palpitations: same-day review and ECG
psychosocial: Closing-down behaviour: caravan cancelled, allotment given away, funeral plans; check mood
Keeping the diagnosis from his wife of 40 years
Belief drawn from a colleague’s death
ice: Idea: “Failure means the engine’s gone. You don’t un-fail.”
Concern: months to live, and protecting Lynne from the news
Expectation: a private number of months to plan around

playbook.diagnosis: Newly diagnosed heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 33%), symptomatic on moderate exertion, congestion improved on furosemide; on low-dose ramipril. Significant distress based on a mistaken belief about prognosis.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your heart’s pump is weaker than it should be. It isn’t finished, it’s under-performing. The medicines we build up over the next few weeks help it work better and often help it recover some strength.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been planning for a timeline you took from Des and from one frightening word. Let’s plan for your heart instead, starting with Scotland in September.”
management.psychosocial: Reinstate the caravan with an August checkpoint; offer a joint call with Lynne where the GP explains; check mood again at review.
sharedPlan: Add beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor to the ACE inhibitor, one step at a time (NICE NG106, TA679, TA773)
U&E before and after each step; BP and pulse; heart failure nurse and cardiac rehabilitation referrals
Flu and pneumococcal vaccination; daily weights; stay active
safetyNet: Weight up more than 2 kg in 3 days, breathless at rest or more pillows: same-day call; chest pain: 999
Bloods next week; GP review in two weeks with Lynne invited; repeat echo after titration

pitfalls.intro: This station looks like a medication review and is really a prognosis conversation. It is failed by ignoring his question, answering it with a number, or never finding what he has already cancelled.

items.fail: Listing drug names and doses without explaining that they change the heart.
items.why: He believes treatment only eases decline; an unexplained list will not be taken as intended.
items.fix: Explain the four classes as the rebuild, furosemide as symptom relief, and the titration with the nurse.

items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG106 requires renal function and potassium checks around ACE inhibitor and MRA changes.
items.fix: Bloods before and after each step, BP and pulse, and a named nurse.

items.fail: Giving a number of months, or deflecting the question entirely.
items.why: A number is false precision; deflection feels like confirmation of the worst.
items.fix: Answer honestly: serious if untreated, much better on treatment, measured by repeat scan rather than guessed.

items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” It hides the cancelled caravan and funeral planning.
items.fix: Ask what he has already done, then reverse it: un-cancel the caravan with an August checkpoint.

items.fail: Telling him he must tell Lynne, or not mentioning her at all.
items.why: Pressure breaches his autonomy; silence leaves the secret costing him sleep.
items.fix: Offer a joint call where the GP explains, at his pace.

items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement in heart failure, where early decompensation is detectable.
items.fix: Daily weights with a threshold, named same-day triggers, chest pain 999, dated bloods and review.

Stairs, pillows, ankles, chest pain, syncope. Then the caravan, allotment, folder, funeral plans, and a brief mood check.
Where the belief came from, and what Lynne has been told.
Under-performing, not finished. Four medicines built up with the nurse. No fake number; measured, not guessed. Des distinguished.
Un-cancel the caravan, August checkpoint. Offer to explain to Lynne. Daily weights, triggers, referrals, dated review.

wordPics.fail: Gives a number of months or refuses the question; lists drug names without explaining the purpose; never finds the cancelled caravan or the secret from Lynne; no titration or monitoring plan; no safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Explains HFrEF and that treatment improves outlook, outlines the four drug classes with titration and blood monitoring, refers to the heart failure nurse, answers prognosis without a number and gives basic safety-netting.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: dismantles the word “failure”; finds and gently reverses the shutdown; distinguishes Des with specifics; sets the caravan as a clinical goal with an August checkpoint; offers to explain to Lynne on the next call; checks mood; uses teach-back that rehearses the disclosure.

avoid.instead: “I won’t guess a number. Untreated this is serious; you won’t be untreated, and your scan will tell us your course.”
avoid.why: Population statistics from before modern treatment are neither accurate for him nor helpful.

avoid.instead: “It’s your decision. If you’d like, she joins the next call and I do the explaining.”
avoid.why: Pressure breaches his autonomy; a practical offer makes disclosure possible.

SCA_MODELS.text: I could ring them tomorrow.

And Lynne. It’s your decision and I’ll respect it. But she’s worrying about “a bit of fluid” while you price funerals alone. If you’d like, she joins our next call and I do the explaining. You just hold her hand while she hears that this is being treated.
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses the secret at his pace with a practical offer

SCA_MODELS.text: (Quietly.) That would help. I didn’t know how to start.

Practical things. Weigh yourself each morning after the toilet, before breakfast. If you go up more than 2 kg in 3 days, get breathless at rest or need more pillows, ring us that day. Chest pain is 999. I’ll refer you to the heart failure nurse and cardiac rehab, bloods next week, and I’ll see you both in two weeks.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific triggers, named referrals and a dated review

SCA_MODELS.text: When Lynne asks tonight how it went, what will you tell her?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back that also rehearses the disclosure

SCA_MODELS.text: That it’s my heart, it’s weak but it can get better, there are four tablets to build up, and the doctor wants to talk to her. And that we’re going to Scotland.

SCA_STEM.name: Trevor Mott
pmh: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, new (LVEF 33% on echo last week)
SCA_STEM.recent: Six weeks of breathlessness and ankle swelling; raised NT-proBNP; echo LVEF 33%. Cardiology letter: GP to start and titrate standard therapy; refer to community heart failure nurse. Retired postman. Wife Lynne usually attends with him.
SCA_STEM.reason: Booked review to discuss the diagnosis and treatment plan.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG106 (chronic heart failure in adults, updated September 2025) · NICE TA679 and TA773 (SGLT2 inhibitors in HFrEF) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: New HFrEF is treatable, and the heart can recover some function with treatment. Four drug classes each improve survival; build them up with the heart failure nurse, and answer the prognosis question honestly without a made-up number.

points.t: NICE NG106: offer an ACE inhibitor (or ARB if not tolerated), a beta-blocker licensed for heart failure, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin, NICE TA679 and TA773) to people with HFrEF. Sacubitril valsartan replaces the ACE inhibitor on specialist advice.

Introduce and titrate one step at a time. NICE NG106: check sodium, potassium and renal function before and after starting an ACE inhibitor or MRA and after each dose increase. Check pulse and BP with beta-blocker titration.
Furosemide treats congestion and symptoms; it is not one of the survival treatments. Adjust to the lowest dose that keeps him dry.
Avoid numbers. Outcomes on full treatment are much better than untreated; ejection fraction often improves after titration, and a repeat echo shows which course he is on.

NICE NG106: offer a personalised, exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation programme; annual flu vaccination and one-off pneumococcal vaccination. Daily weights: ESC 2021 advises acting on a rise of more than 2 kg in 3 days. DVLA Group 1: he may drive and need not notify unless symptoms distract him.
Breathlessness at rest, new orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal breathlessness, rapid weight gain, syncope: same-day review. Chest pain: 999. New palpitations: ECG, as AF changes management.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Let him ask his question first, promised an honest answer, and agreed confidentiality and an agenda.
Retired postman, married 40 years, bowls, allotment; the cancelled caravan and the plans he has been quietly making.
Picked up “things I need to organise”, joining alone and early, and the Lynne secret, and explored each.
Idea (failure means finished, based on Des), concern (months to live and protecting Lynne), expectation (a private number).
U&E before and after each titration step, BP and pulse, weight; repeat echo after titration; NT-proBNP trend as advised.
Checked current congestion and function (NYHA class, orthopnoea) and separated sleeplessness from breathlessness.
Asked about chest pain, syncope and rest breathlessness; checked mood and self-harm given the closing-down behaviour.
Explained HFrEF as an under-performing pump that can improve, not a finished one.
Four core drug classes per NICE NG106, started low and titrated with the heart failure nurse; furosemide explained as symptom relief; caravan set as a goal.
Cardiac rehabilitation, flu and pneumococcal vaccination, activity encouraged, driving advice; the Lynne conversation offered.
Daily weights with a threshold, same-day triggers, chest pain 999, bloods booked, two-week review with Lynne invited.

social.t: Withholding a diagnosis to protect a partner leaves the patient carrying it alone and the partner excluded. Offer to help with disclosure; do not force it.
Cancelling plans, giving away hobbies and arranging paperwork can reflect despair built on a mistaken prognosis. Correcting the belief is part of treatment.

legal.t: He is entitled to decide who is told about his diagnosis (GMC Confidentiality 2017). Record his wishes and any later consent to share with Lynne.
Group 1: heart failure need not be reported unless symptoms may distract the driver. Group 2 rules differ (LVEF below 40% is a bar).

professional.t: Answer the prognosis question truthfully without false precision or false reassurance (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Cardiology has asked the GP to initiate and titrate. Agree responsibilities with the heart failure nurse and document the titration plan.

community.t: Community heart failure nurse, cardiac rehabilitation, British Heart Foundation information for patients and partners, and the Pumping Marvellous Foundation for peer support.

redFlags: Breathlessness at rest, new orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal breathlessness: same-day review
Rapid weight gain, syncope, new palpitations: same-day review and ECG
psychosocial: Closing-down behaviour: caravan cancelled, allotment given away, funeral plans; check mood
Keeping the diagnosis from his wife of 40 years
Belief drawn from a colleague’s death
ice: Idea: “Failure means the engine’s gone. You don’t un-fail.”
Concern: months to live, and protecting Lynne from the news
Expectation: a private number of months to plan around

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Newly diagnosed heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 33%), symptomatic on moderate exertion, congestion improved on furosemide; on low-dose ramipril. Significant distress based on a mistaken belief about prognosis.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your heart’s pump is weaker than it should be. It isn’t finished, it’s under-performing. The medicines we build up over the next few weeks help it work better and often help it recover some strength.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been planning for a timeline you took from Des and from one frightening word. Let’s plan for your heart instead, starting with Scotland in September.”
management.psychosocial: Reinstate the caravan with an August checkpoint; offer a joint call with Lynne where the GP explains; check mood again at review.
sharedPlan: Add beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor to the ACE inhibitor, one step at a time (NICE NG106, TA679, TA773)
U&E before and after each step; BP and pulse; heart failure nurse and cardiac rehabilitation referrals
Flu and pneumococcal vaccination; daily weights; stay active
safetyNet: Weight up more than 2 kg in 3 days, breathless at rest or more pillows: same-day call; chest pain: 999
Bloods next week; GP review in two weeks with Lynne invited; repeat echo after titration

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station looks like a medication review and is really a prognosis conversation. It is failed by ignoring his question, answering it with a number, or never finding what he has already cancelled.

items.fail: Listing drug names and doses without explaining that they change the heart.
items.why: He believes treatment only eases decline; an unexplained list will not be taken as intended.
items.fix: Explain the four classes as the rebuild, furosemide as symptom relief, and the titration with the nurse.

items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG106 requires renal function and potassium checks around ACE inhibitor and MRA changes.
items.fix: Bloods before and after each step, BP and pulse, and a named nurse.

items.fail: Giving a number of months, or deflecting the question entirely.
items.why: A number is false precision; deflection feels like confirmation of the worst.
items.fix: Answer honestly: serious if untreated, much better on treatment, measured by repeat scan rather than guessed.

items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” It hides the cancelled caravan and funeral planning.
items.fix: Ask what he has already done, then reverse it: un-cancel the caravan with an August checkpoint.

items.fail: Telling him he must tell Lynne, or not mentioning her at all.
items.why: Pressure breaches his autonomy; silence leaves the secret costing him sleep.
items.fix: Offer a joint call where the GP explains, at his pace.

items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement in heart failure, where early decompensation is detectable.
items.fix: Daily weights with a threshold, named same-day triggers, chest pain 999, dated bloods and review.
